title: DOJ Withdraws Subpoenas Against New York Times Reporters After Judge’s Sharp Rebuke
excerpt: Federal judge Arun Subramanian grilled prosecutors for 90 minutes over subpoenas targeting journalists who reported on security flaws in a Qatari-donated Air Force One jet.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DOJ withdrew subpoenas against New York Times reporters after a judge's intense questioning.
  • Judge Arun Subramanian emphasized high legal standards for compelling journalists to reveal sources.
  • Subpoenas included demands for phone records of reporters' family members, which prosecutors later admitted was an error.
  • The case highlights ongoing tensions between the Trump administration and press freedom regarding classified information.
  • DOJ withdrew subpoenas against New York Times journalists after a federal judge questioned their legal procedures.
  • The judge emphasized that compelling journalists to reveal sources requires a high legal threshold.
  • The subpoenas were issued following a Times article about security concerns regarding a Qatari plane gifted for Air Force One.
  • The withdrawal is seen as a victory for press freedom advocates and a response to the judge's scrutiny.

The Justice Department abruptly withdrew subpoenas issued to New York Times journalists on Thursday after a federal judge sharply questioned prosecutors about whether they had followed legal procedures — a retreat that press freedom advocates called a vindication of First Amendment protections.

“The government is prepared to unilaterally withdraw the subpoenas at this time,” prosecutor Sean Buckley told U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian during a hearing in lower Manhattan, adding that the investigation remained ongoing and the government could reissue subpoenas.

Judge Grills DOJ for 90 Minutes

The withdrawal came after Subramanian, a Biden appointee, spent roughly 90 minutes pressing government lawyers on procedural issues. The judge made clear that compelling journalists to reveal their sources carries a high legal threshold.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=-LBALGCEhGg

“They are the last thing you do. It’s a matter of basic compliance with the law.”

— Judge Arun Subramanian, U.S. District Court

CNN analyst Andrew McCabe said the judge “made it absolutely clear” he would have quashed the subpoenas had the DOJ not withdrawn them voluntarily — framing the move as damage control rather than a change of heart.

The Reporting That Sparked the Probe

Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton — Trump’s nominee for Director of National Intelligence — issued the subpoenas on July 10, just two days after the Times published an article reporting that government officials had security concerns about a Boeing 747 gifted by Qatar for use as Air Force One.

Subpoena Controversy Unfolds
July 10, 2023

July 12, 2023
Judge Arun Subramanian questions DOJ for 90 minutes about the subpoenas.
July 13, 2023
DOJ withdraws subpoenas after judge's rebuke, but investigation remains ongoing.
https://x.com/OccupyDemocrats/status/2080393150896701865

The reporting revealed that Trump departed a NATO summit in Turkey on the older presidential aircraft because the Qatari plane lacked antimissile defenses and other protective features standard on the existing fleet. The stories, which cited anonymous sources, coincided with the collapse of a ceasefire in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

Trump privately seethed over the coverage of the plane’s security gaps, CNN reported. The Justice Department opened a leak investigation and took aggressive steps to identify officials who had spoken to the Times, including confiscating cell phones at the White House.

Subpoenas Delivered by Armed Agents

Armed FBI agents served grand jury subpoenas at the homes of three Times reporters, demanding testimony about the Air Force One coverage. Prosecutors also issued a second round of subpoenas seeking phone records — some tied to reporters’ relatives.

Court filings revealed the phone records request extended to one reporter’s mother, described as a mental health professional with confidential client relationships, and the spouses of two other reporters. Buckley acknowledged the inclusion of family members was an error from pulling numbers too broadly from a law enforcement database.

“That was an error, judge, which we own,” Buckley said. “It was a consequence of trying to move quickly.”

Press Freedom at a Crossroads

The Times had fought the subpoenas aggressively, filing a motion describing them as “a bad faith effort to harass and intimidate” journalists and arguing they violated internal DOJ policies requiring top-level approval before subpoenaing reporters.

David McCraw, the Times’ top newsroom lawyer, said: “We are pleased that the government finally conceded that the subpoenas violated the law, but they should never have been issued in the first place.”

The Freedom of the Press Foundation condemned the targeting of reporters’ families. “Even the Mafia says families are off limits,” said chief of advocacy Seth Stern.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee last week that he personally authorized the journalists’ subpoenas — a disclosure that added political weight to the legal battle.

An Indian-American Judge at the Center

Judge Subramanian, an Indian-American jurist appointed to the Southern District of New York by President Biden, has emerged as a prominent figure in cases testing the boundaries of executive power. His pointed questioning during Thursday’s hearing underscored the judiciary’s role in checking government overreach against the press.

The withdrawal does not end the investigation. Subramanian noted prosecutors could return with new subpoenas if they follow proper procedures — leaving the door open for another confrontation between the administration and the newspaper.

Impact on Press Freedom
›Judge's questioning highlighted legal protections for journalists.
›Subpoenas targeted reporters' families, raising ethical concerns.
›Times described subpoenas as harassment and intimidation.
›Freedom of the Press Foundation condemned targeting of families.
nri_angle: Indian-American Judge Arun Subramanian played a pivotal role in the outcome, emerging as a key judicial figure in cases testing executive power and press freedom.
